questions.q: What was the 'quiet, embarrassing problem' that hinted at a missing particle in the nucleus before 1932?
options: Hydrogen was lighter than its single proton predicted
Helium is four times as heavy as hydrogen, yet has only twice the charge — so its two protons cannot account for all its mass
Electrons were found to be heavier than protons
Gamma rays were too penetrating to measure accurately
questions.explanation: Helium has twice hydrogen's charge (two protons) but four times its mass. The protons account for only half the mass, so something heavy and chargeless had to be present in the nucleus — the missing mass that pointed to the neutron.

questions.q: Why was a neutral particle almost impossible to detect with 1920s apparatus?
options: It moved too slowly to register on any detector
Detection relied on charge — a charged particle ionises gas and leaves a curving track, but a neutral particle ionises nothing and leaves no trail
It was absorbed instantly by the cloud chamber walls
Magnetic fields destroyed neutral particles on contact
questions.explanation: The whole toolkit relied on charge: a charged particle rips electrons off atoms, leaving a visible ionisation trail that curves in a magnetic field. A neutral particle leaves no trail and curves in no field — it glides through 'like a ghost through a wall'.

questions.q: Why did quantum mechanics reject the idea that electrons were buried inside the nucleus to cancel charge?
options: Electrons have no mass, so they could not contribute to the nucleus
Confining an electron to a space a few femtometres across would require an enormous energy — its quantum wavelength was simply too large to fit
Electrons are repelled by protons and could never enter the nucleus
The nucleus was already full of protons with no room left
questions.explanation: The new quantum mechanics showed that squeezing an electron into a nucleus-sized space demanded an impossibly large energy because its wavelength was too big — 'like trying to keep an ocean wave inside a teacup'. The nuclear-electron idea was a fudge.

questions.q: What mistake did Bothe and Becker, and later the Joliot-Curies, make about the beryllium radiation?
options: They measured the proton speeds incorrectly
They interpreted the penetrating, chargeless radiation as gamma rays — reaching for a familiar explanation rather than a new particle
They believed it was a beam of fast electrons
They thought it was ordinary alpha particles reflected from the beryllium
questions.explanation: Their experiments were sound — the penetration and neutrality were real — but they labelled the radiation 'gamma rays' because that was the familiar neutral radiation. That single wrong word sent others chasing a contradiction they could not resolve.

questions.q: Why is a gamma-ray photon a poor candidate for knocking a fast proton out of paraffin wax?
options: Photons cannot travel through wax at all
For a given energy a photon carries very little momentum (\(p = E/c\)), so it transfers momentum to a heavy proton very inefficiently
Photons are repelled by the positive charge of the proton
Gamma rays only interact with electrons, never with protons
questions.explanation: A photon's momentum is its energy divided by the speed of light, so it is 'momentum-poor'. Shoving a heavy proton with a photon is 'like knocking over a bowling ball with a ping-pong ball' — you would need an absurd photon energy.

questions.q: What kind of projectile transfers its speed most efficiently to a proton in a head-on elastic collision?
options: A very heavy particle, far more massive than the proton
A particle with roughly the same mass as the proton, which can hand over almost all its speed — like equal billiard balls
A massless particle such as a photon
A particle much lighter than the proton, like an electron
questions.explanation: Two equal masses pass momentum cleanly: the projectile can stop dead and hand almost all its speed to the target, like a cue ball striking an equal ball head-on. So a neutral particle of about a proton's mass explains the fast protons with no miracle energy.

questions.q: Why did the neutron become 'the perfect tool' for probing and transforming the nucleus, leading to nuclear fission?
options: It was the fastest particle ever produced in a laboratory
Having no charge, it feels no electrical repulsion from a positive nucleus and can drift right in, however gently
It carried far more energy than any alpha particle
It could only be absorbed by light elements, never heavy ones
questions.explanation: Charged projectiles must be fired hard to overcome a nucleus's electrical repulsion, but the neutron has no charge, so that wall does not exist for it. It can slip into a nucleus and rearrange it — the basis of the 1938 discovery of nuclear fission.

questions.q: From memory: lay out the energy argument Chadwick used to rule out gamma rays as the beryllium radiation.
keyPoints: To eject the protons at their measured speed, a gamma-ray photon would need an energy of about 50 million electron volts (50 MeV).
The only energy source was the incident alpha particles, which supplied only about 5 MeV.
Demanding 50 MeV from a 5 MeV reaction — a tenfold increase — is a flat violation of conservation of energy, so the gamma-ray explanation is impossible.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the ~50 MeV required versus the ~5 MeV available, and named conservation of energy as the law broken, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: how did the discovery of the neutron resolve the helium mass problem and explain isotopes?
keyPoints: Helium's nucleus is two protons plus two neutrons — four particles each about a proton's mass, giving mass 4 and charge 2.
The number of protons fixes the charge and chemistry; protons plus neutrons fix the mass.
Isotopes are atoms with the same number of protons (same chemistry) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass).
questions.explanation: The crux is separating charge (set by protons) from mass (set by protons plus neutrons). If you linked both the helium 'four-times' puzzle and isotopes to neutron number, grade it Good or Easy.

questions.q: The gamma-ray hypothesis required each photon to carry about 50 MeV, but the alpha particles striking the beryllium supplied only about 5 MeV. By what factor does the gamma-ray story exceed the available energy, and what does that prove?
questions.given: Energy required by gamma-ray hypothesis \(\approx 50\,\mathrm{MeV}\); energy available from alpha particles \(\approx 5\,\mathrm{MeV}\)
working: The hypothesis demands ten times more energy than the reaction can supply — energy from nowhere — which violates conservation of energy, so the radiation cannot be gamma rays.
questions.explanation: Dividing the required energy by the available energy gives a factor of 10. You cannot pour 50 units of energy from a jug holding 5 — a flat violation of conservation of energy, the killing blow against the gamma-ray explanation.

questions.q: Explain why the high speed of the protons ejected from the paraffin wax was evidence against the gamma-ray hypothesis, and how it pointed instead to a neutral particle of mass similar to that of a proton. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Energy argument: to eject the protons at their measured speed, a gamma-ray photon would need an energy of about 50 MeV, but the incident alpha particles supply only about 5 MeV. Demanding ten times more energy than the reaction can provide violates the conservation of energy, ruling photons out. Momentum argument: a photon carries very little momentum for its energy (p = E/c), so it is extremely inefficient at shoving a heavy proton forward. A neutral particle of mass close to the proton's, however, transfers momentum to a proton with great efficiency — like two equal billiard balls colliding head-on. Applying conservation of energy and conservation of momentum together therefore not only rules out the photon but forces the conclusion of a massive neutral particle: the neutron.

criteria.descriptor: States the gamma-ray hypothesis needs ~50 MeV per photon while only ~5 MeV is available.
Identifies this as a violation of conservation of energy, ruling out photons.
Explains a photon carries little momentum for its energy, so transfers momentum to a proton inefficiently.
Concludes a neutral particle of mass close to the proton's transfers momentum efficiently (equal-mass elastic collision), as required by conservation of momentum.

questions.explanation: Full marks require both laws: conservation of energy to kill the photon, and conservation of momentum (efficient equal-mass transfer) to demand a proton-mass neutral particle.
